title: Agent frameworks: orchestration patterns and when you need one
hook: A framework can save you from rebuilding common plumbing, but it also adds a layer you don't fully control; know what problem you actually have before reaching for one.
inPlainWords: Agent frameworks come in different shapes: a graph of steps you can inspect, a set of roles that hand off to each other, or a lighter library for composing prompts and tools. Pick the shape that matches your actual pain, not the most popular name.

useCase.title: Should the team build the agent loop from scratch, or use a framework?
useCase.story: The complaint-investigating agent needs to call tools, keep state across steps, and sometimes hand off between specialized roles. A team member suggests adopting a popular agent framework. Another argues a few hundred lines of custom code would be simpler and easier to debug.

approaches.name: Hand-rolled loop
approaches.what: Write the core loop yourself: the model proposes an action, code executes it, the result goes back in, repeat until done.
approaches.greatWhen: The pattern is simple, and the team wants full visibility into every step for debugging.
approaches.avoidWhen: The system grows many tools, roles and edge cases, and the hand-rolled plumbing starts duplicating what frameworks already solved.
approaches.example: A 200-line loop that's easy to read and step through.

approaches.name: A graph or state-machine orchestrator
approaches.what: A framework that lets you define the agent's steps and transitions explicitly, as a graph, so control flow is visible and steppable.
approaches.greatWhen: The workflow has clear states and transitions you want to see and control precisely, especially with loops or branches.
approaches.avoidWhen: The workflow is simple linear steps that don't need explicit state management.
approaches.example: A graph with nodes for "investigate," "decide," "escalate," and explicit edges between them.

approaches.name: A role-based multi-agent framework
approaches.what: A framework built around defining multiple agents with roles that hand off or collaborate, with built-in coordination.
approaches.greatWhen: The task genuinely splits into distinct roles that benefit from separate prompts and tools.
approaches.avoidWhen: One well-prompted agent already handles the task, since splitting adds coordination overhead for no benefit.
approaches.example: A "reader" role and a "decider" role handing off, after a single agent kept conflating the two jobs.

approaches.name: A code-first chaining library
approaches.what: A lighter framework focused on composing prompts, tools and calls as code, without full graph or multi-agent machinery.
approaches.greatWhen: You want reusable building blocks, like prompt templates and tool wrappers, without adopting a heavier orchestration model.
approaches.avoidWhen: You need explicit state and control flow visibility that a chaining library doesn't provide.
approaches.example: A shared tool wrapper is reused across three small agent scripts, with no shared state machine needed.

approaches.name: Evaluate by what breaks, not by popularity
approaches.what: Choose based on your actual pain point, such as debugging visibility, role separation, or reusable plumbing, not which framework is trending.
approaches.example: The team names the exact plumbing problem before comparing any framework's feature list.

challenge.question: The agent's control flow has grown to include loops, branches and an escalation path that's getting hard to trace in a hand-rolled loop. What should guide the next step?

options.text: Move to a graph or state-machine orchestrator that makes the states and transitions explicit and steppable, since the actual pain is invisible control flow
options.why: It directly addresses the stated problem, tracing loops and branches, rather than adding machinery for a different problem.

options.text: Adopt a role-based multi-agent framework because it's popular
options.why: The problem described is control-flow visibility, not a need for multiple specialized roles; this doesn't fix the actual pain.

options.text: Keep extending the hand-rolled loop indefinitely
options.why: Possible, but the team already reports it's getting hard to trace, and a purpose-built tool for exactly this problem exists.

options.text: Rewrite everything in a code-first chaining library
options.why: Chaining libraries help reuse prompt and tool code, but don't solve the state and branch visibility problem described.

bestCase.title: Picking the framework that matches the actual pain
bestCase.example: The team adopts a graph orchestrator, redraws the investigation flow as explicit nodes and edges, and a teammate can now point to exactly which state a stuck case is in, instead of reading through nested conditionals.

worstCase.title: Framework shopping instead of diagnosing
worstCase.example: The team adopts a trending multi-agent framework because of its popularity, splits the single working agent into three roles that now need to coordinate, and spends a month debugging handoff bugs that didn't exist before.

route.travelling: The complaint-investigating agent's growing control flow

steps.label: Name the actual pain
steps.goes: Loops and branches are hard to trace in the current code.

steps.label: Match the pain to a pattern
steps.goes: State and transition visibility, not multiple roles, is needed.
steps.goesWrong: The team picks a multi-agent framework because it's popular, not because roles are the actual problem.

steps.label: Adopt a graph orchestrator
steps.goes: States and transitions become explicit nodes and edges.

steps.label: Redraw the existing flow
steps.goes: Investigate, decide, escalate become visible, steppable nodes.

steps.label: Debug a stuck case
steps.goes: A teammate points to the exact stuck state in seconds.

takeaway: Pick an agent framework for the specific plumbing problem you actually have, control-flow visibility, role separation, or reusable pieces, not for its popularity.
